title: The Market’s Fed Watch in Action | Dimensional
author: Wes Crill, PhD, Senior Client Solutions Director and Vice President
text:
Perspectives The Market’s Fed Watch in Action By Wes Crill, PhD, Senior Client Solutions Director and Vice President The Market’s Fed Watch in Action View All Insights

Sep 24, 2026 1 Minute Read Topic Economic Perspectives Fixed Income Investing Inflation

The US Federal Reserve announced on Wednesday its decision to raise the federal-funds rate 25 basis points. But investors expecting a big reaction in bond yields might have been surprised. A Fed rate hike wasn’t always a foregone conclusion. As recently as May 1, fed-funds futures pricing implied a near-zero probability of rates going up at the September meeting. But an unexpectedly high September consumer price index (CPI) print was followed by the rate hike probability cresting 90%.1 Treasury yields appeared to signal the anticipation of a rate increase. For example, the one-year US Treasury yield jumped by about 22 bps in the days surrounding the CPI release—roughly equivalent to the magnitude of the eventual hike. The yield then leveled off until the Fed’s announcement, rising again slightly amid signals of another possible increase this year. This demonstrates the forward-looking nature of markets, pricing in the Fed’s actions before they take place. Footnotes

1. Rate hike probabilities are based on the CME Group’s FedWatch Tool.

Glossary

Basis points: One basis point equals 0.01%. Consumer price index (CPI): Measures the change in prices paid by consumers for goods and services. Federal-funds rate: Target interest rate range set by the US Federal Reserve that commercial banks charge each other for overnight loans of their excess reserve balances. Treasury yields: The yields on US Treasury securities.
